---
title: Reproducibility
guide-section: "Reproducible requests"
---

A trialforge study is a pure function of its request: the archetype, `n`, the seed, `studyid`{.gd-no-link},
the controls and the defects. The same request gives byte-identical files on every platform, and
from Python and R alike. Nothing else goes in: not the time, the machine, the DataFrame backend or
the order in which studies were generated.

That makes a study something you can refer to rather than store. A test suite can regenerate its
fixtures instead of checking in megabytes of XPT, a bug report can say "seed 41, 200 subjects", and
a colleague using R can look at the same data you see in Python.

## Seeds

Pass `seed=` to fix a study. With no seed, trialforge draws a fresh one and records it, so any study
can be reproduced later:

```{python}
import polars as pl
import trialforge as tf

trial = tf.study("vaccine", n=100)
trial.seed
```

```{python}
again = tf.study("vaccine", n=100, seed=trial.seed)
again.define_xml("sdtm") == trial.define_xml("sdtm") and again.truth == trial.truth
```

The seed is also in the [truth manifest](04-truth.qmd) and in the summary line of the study, so a
`truth.json` written next to the files is enough to regenerate them.

Seeds are whole numbers from 0 to `tf.MAX_SEED` (2^53, the largest range of integers that R's
doubles hold exactly, so a seed means the same in both languages):

```{python}
tf.MAX_SEED
```

Neighboring seeds give unrelated studies: there is no sense in which seed 2 is close to seed 1.

## Random streams

Every random draw comes from a stream addressed by a path under the root seed: the subject, then the
process (adverse events, labs, dropout), then the analyte or term. Because each independent process
has its own stream, changing one part of a study disturbs only what depends on it. More missed
visits change the visits and the measurements taken at them, but not the subjects, their adverse
events or their medical history:

```{python}
base = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1)
more_missed = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1, missed_visit=0.2)
{name: base.sdtm[name].equals(more_missed.sdtm[name]) for name in ("DM", "AE", "MH", "SV", "VS")}
```

`tf.stream_seed()` gives the seed of the stream at a path. Integers in the path are indices and
strings are labels:

```{python}
tf.stream_seed(1, ["subject", 17, "ae"])
```

You don't need stream seeds to use trialforge; they are there to explain, and to test, which draws
a change can reach.

## What a control changes

A control changes the datasets that depend on what it controls, and nothing else. Here are four
controls of a hypertension study, each changed on its own, with the SDTM datasets that change:

```{python}
def changed(**controls: object) -> list[str]:
    base = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1, indication="hypertension")
    other = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1, indication="hypertension", **controls)
    return [name for name in base.sdtm if not base.sdtm[name].equals(other.sdtm[name])]


{
    "change": changed(change=[-4, -15]),
    "missed_visit": changed(missed_visit=0.2),
    "ae_rate_multiplier": changed(ae_rate_multiplier=3.0),
    "dropout_rate": changed(dropout_rate=0.3),
}
```

- A larger treatment effect only moves the post-baseline blood pressures in VS. The subjects, their
visits, adverse events and labs are the same.
- More missed visits remove visits (SV) and with them the measurements (LB, VS) and the study drug
dispensed at them (EX).
- More adverse events change AE and SUPPAE, and CM, where medications are taken for them. They
reach further, because an adverse event can lead to discontinuation: those subjects' participation
ends earlier, which changes their reference end dates (DM), disposition (DS), elements (SE), visits,
exposure, and every record after the new end date.
- A higher dropout rate ends more subjects' participation early, with the same reach.

Medical history is drawn before treatment from each subject's own stream, so it is unchanged in all
four. The trial design datasets (TA, TE, TV, TI, TS) depend only on the design.

`studyid`{.gd-no-link} changes no random draw: a study with another identifier has the same data,
with the new `STUDYID` and the subject identifiers built from it.

## What changing `n` changes

Each subject's own draws (their site, age, sex, race, ethnicity, enrollment date, medical history
and the course of their disease) come from the subject's stream, so they don't depend on how many
other subjects there are. Two things are study-level sequences instead, as in a real study:

- **Subject numbers**: `SUBJID` is the site number and the subject's place in the site's
  enrollment order, so a subject enrolled earlier at the same site moves everyone after them up one.
- **Arm assignment**: randomization is in permuted blocks, in enrollment order, so a new subject
  takes a slot in a block and shifts the assignments after it.

Compare a 300-subject study with the same request for 301. Subjects are matched on their baseline
characteristics:

```{python}
small = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1)
large = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=301, seed=1)

baseline = ["SITEID", "RFICDTC", "AGE", "SEX", "RACE", "ETHNIC"]
pairs = small.sdtm["DM"].join(large.sdtm["DM"], on=baseline, suffix="_301")
pairs.select(
    matched=pl.len(),
    same_usubjid=(pl.col("USUBJID") == pl.col("USUBJID_301")).sum(),
    same_arm=(pl.col("ARM") == pl.col("ARM_301")).sum(),
)
```

All 300 subjects are still there, with the same baseline. The extra subject enrolled early at site
205, so the few subjects enrolled after them at that site were renumbered, and the block slots of
everyone randomized after them (in the same stratum, where there are strata) shifted, changing many
of their arms. A subject's medical history, baseline measurements
and the random parts of their course are the same whatever their arm, so a subject who keeps their
arm keeps their data; one whose arm changed gets that arm's treatment effect and adverse event
rates.

So a study with more subjects is a different study, not the same one extended. To compare designs on
the same subjects, keep `n` and the seed fixed and change the controls.

## Across platforms and languages

trialforge doesn't use the platform's math library for random values (implementations differ in
the last bit from one system to the next) but a pure-Rust one, and its random draws are defined by
the engine, not by Python or R. Golden test cases pin the XPT bytes of reference studies: the Python
package is tested against them on Linux, macOS and Windows, and the R package replays the same
cases.

The R package gives the same data for the same request:

```r
library(trialforge)
trial <- study("vaccine", n = 100, seed = 1)
```

R row numbers count from 1 and Python's from 0; `defects.json` is zero-based in both.

The DataFrame backend doesn't matter either: `output="pandas"` and `output="pyarrow"` hold the same
values as Polars, and the files written are the same whichever you chose.

## Across releases

The data for a given request can change between trialforge releases, when a model or a derivation
is improved; the changelog says when it does. To reproduce a study exactly, record the trialforge
version with the seed and controls:

```{python}
tf.__version__, tf.core_version()
```

`tf.core_version()` is the version of the Rust engine that generated the data. A
[study spec](08-study-specs.qmd) together with the version is a complete record of a study.
